It discovers public IP addresses, virtual machines, and load balancers across your AWS environments, identifies reachable ports, and determines what services are running behind them. This complements Security Hub's existing network reachability findings, which identify configurations that could make a resource reachable from the internet. Network Scanning confirms that configurations do exist which make a resource reachable from the internet. Each reachable port generates a Security Hub finding with evidence of the port and service discovered. Security Hub Exposures then automatically correlates these findings with other findings and resource configurations to determine broader risk. Existing customers can enable Network Scanning in individual accounts and regions, or across an organization via a configuration policy. For new Security Hub customers, Network Scanning is on by default. Network Scanning is included with Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost in all AWS commercial and GovCloud (US) Regions that support Security Hub. To learn more, see the AWS Security Hub User Guide and the AWS Security Hub product page . For the full list of Regions, see the AWS Regional Services List .

items.title: AWS Lambda durable functions increases default execution and API quotas
items.description: AWS Lambda durable functions has increased default quotas for running executions and API request rates. The new quotas below apply in all AWS Regions except US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), and Europe (Ireland), which have twice these quotas. Running durable executions per account (1 million to 5 million) Function invocation rate to start durable executions (300 to 3,000 requests per second) CheckpointDurableExecution and GetDurableExecutionState (1,000 to 10,000 requests per second) SendDurableExecutionCallbackSuccess, SendDurableExecutionCallbackFailure, and SendDurableExecutionCallbackHeartbeat (300 to 3,000 requests per second) GetDurableExecution and StopDurableExecution (30 to 300 requests per second) GetDurableExecutionHistory and ListDurableExecutionsByFunction (15 to 150 requests per second) AWS Lambda durable functions helps you build resilient multi-step applications and AI workflows that execute for up to one year, with built-in checkpointing, automatic retries, and waits that suspend execution without incurring compute charges. With this increase, workloads such as order processing and document pipelines can run more executions in parallel without requesting quota increases. When many executions wait on external work, such as payment confirmations or batch jobs, more can resume together. If you monitor and manage executions with your dashboards or scripts, they can now check status, list executions, read history, and stop executions at least ten times as often. The new quotas apply in all AWS Regions where AWS Lambda durable functions is available. To learn more, see Lambda quotas in the AWS Lambda Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS CodeConnections is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region
items.description: AWS CodeConnections is now available in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) Region, in addition to AWS GovCloud (US-East). CodeConnections lets you connect AWS services such as AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild to source code repositories hosted with third-party providers such as Bitbucket. With this launch, customers running workloads in AWS GovCloud (US-West) can create connections to their source repositories in the same Region as their pipelines. For example, a team can configure a connection so that a commit to their repository automatically starts a release in AWS CodePipeline, without managing provider credentials for each integration. To learn more, see the AWS CodeConnections User Guide and the AWS GovCloud User Guide . To get started, visit the AWS GovCloud (US) console.

items.title: Amazon EC2 now publishes ImdsV1Enabled CloudWatch metric
items.description: Amazon EC2 now supports an ImdsV1Enabled CloudWatch metric, giving customers visibility into which of their EC2 instances still have Instance Metadata Service Version 1 (IMDSv1) enabled. You can use this metric to track your migration to IMDSv2 across your accounts and Regions, at scale. With the ImdsV1Enabled metric, you can configure CloudWatch dashboards and alarms to track instances that still allow IMDSv1, identify migration gaps, and prioritize remediation, without building your own tooling to check the metadata options of instances across accounts and Regions. This gives you a reliable, ongoing signal to track and complete your IMDSv2 migration. The ImdsV1Enabled CloudWatch metric is available in all AWS Regions at no additional cost. To learn more, see the ImdsV1Enabled CloudWatch metric in the Amazon EC2 User Guide . For step-by-step migration instructions, see Transition to IMDSv2 in the Amazon EC2 User Guide .

items.title: Amazon SageMaker AI Studio Now Supports IAM Identity Center Multi-Region Replication
items.description: Amazon SageMaker AI now supports IAM Identity Center (IdC) multi-region replication, enabling you to deploy SageMaker AI Studio domains in different regions from your IdC instance's primary region. Previously, the primary IdC instance had to reside in the same region as the SageMaker AI Studio domain; now customers can replicate their primary IdC instance into the region where they wish to use SageMaker AI Studio domains. This capability helps customers maintain compliance while utilizing centralized workforce identity management. As an Amazon SageMaker AI Studio administrator, you can deploy SageMaker AI domains that align with your workforce's location and data residency requirements, independent of where your primary IdC instance is set up. Organizations can retain their primary IdC instance in one region while operating SageMaker AI Studio workloads in compliance-mandated regions, support global operations through centralized identity management, and satisfy data sovereignty requirements without compromising single sign-on (SSO) capabilities. To get started see the SageMaker AI documentation and to learn about setting up IAM Identity Center multi-region support see the IAM Identity Center User Guide . Multi-region IdC replication is available in all standard AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker AI Studio is supported, including: Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Ireland), US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), South America (São Paulo), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm).

items.title: AWS WAF AI traffic monetization now supports fiat payouts through Stripe
items.description: AWS WAF AI traffic monetization now integrates with Stripe. Publishers, content owners, and API providers can collect stablecoin payments from AI bots and agents that settle in local currency directly to their Stripe balance. With this launch, customers can monetize agent access without holding stablecoins or managing a crypto wallet. Stripe is now available as a new payout method alongside existing stablecoin payouts. To get started, connect your Stripe account to AWS WAF through Stripe Connect in the AWS WAF console. Your existing pricing and agent policies work unchanged. When an agent requests protected content, AWS WAF returns an HTTP 402 response with the valid payment credential types that it accepts. Once the agent returns with a valid payment credential and makes the request again, the content is returned ungated. Revenue from all payment providers appears in the AWS WAF console revenue analytics. The Stripe integration is available at no additional charge to all AWS WAF customers using Amazon CloudFront, in all edge locations where AWS WAF web ACLs are associated with CloudFront distributions. Standard AWS WAF and Stripe processing fees apply. See AWS WAF pricing for details. To get started, visit the AWS WAF console or explore the AWS WAF Developer Guide .

items.title: Amazon Q Developer in console is now the AWS assistant
items.description: Amazon Q Developer in the AWS Management Console and Console Mobile Apps is now called the AWS assistant. Previously, customers interacted with Amazon Q Developer across these surfaces. Now, the AWS assistant provides the same personalized, account-aware guidance and actions with a name that immediately communicates what the product does. The AWS assistant simplifies how customers build, operate, and optimize on AWS. The AWS assistant is currently offered for free. Existing Amazon Q Developer Pro subscribers will automatically retain their Pro Tier capabilities under the AWS assistant. The AWS assistant is available globally. To learn more, visit aws.amazon.com/products/assistant/ .

items.title: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store now allows organization and validation with built-in data types
items.description: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store now supports 13 new parameter data types that automatically validate parameter values when you create or update a parameter. With built-in validation, you can stop malformed configuration values, such as an invalid IP address, AWS account ID, or JSON document, before your applications read them, without writing your own validation logic. These types allow you to better organize your parameters across your workloads. You can filter by type when calling the DescribeParameters API or when browsing parameters in the Parameter Store console. The following data types are available for both standard and advanced parameters:  aws:region, aws:account:id, boolean, integer, float, binary, hostname, email, ipv4-address, and ipv6-address. Three more data types, url, json, and jsonc, are available for advanced parameters. Parameter Store checks the value when you call PutParameter and rejects any value that doesn't match its data type. New data types work with String and SecureString parameters, and several also support StringList parameters, where each item in the list is validated. You can combine a data type with an AllowedPattern for additional constraints, and you can change the data type of an existing text parameter.

items.title: Amazon MWAA now supports cost allocation tags
items.description: Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) now supports cost allocation tags . Tags you apply to an Amazon MWAA environment now propagate to the compute that runs it, including workers, schedulers, and web servers. You can then track Amazon MWAA spend by tag in AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Cost and Usage Reports. With this launch, platform teams can show back or charge back Airflow costs to the team, project, or cost center that owns each environment. You can use cost allocation tags when you create a new environment or update an existing one. To get started, tag your environment using the Amazon MWAA console, AWS CLI, or Amazon MWAA API, then activate the tag key as a cost allocation tag in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon MWAA is available. For more information, see the AWS Region table . To learn more, visit Cost allocation tags in Amazon MWAA in the Amazon MWAA User Guide.

items.title: Amazon ECS Managed Daemons can now collect json-file logs from application containers on Amazon ECS Managed Instances
items.description: Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) introduces json-file log driver support for Amazon ECS Managed Instances and log driver volumes for Amazon ECS Managed Daemons. Together, these features let you collect application logs with the observability agent of your choice and forward them to any destination you choose. With this launch, your application containers on ECS Managed Instances can write their logs as local files in standard Docker json-file format, which most observability agents read natively. Your managed daemons can directly read these files through a volume mount, without specifying host bind mount paths or requiring root privileges. As a result, one managed daemon on each instance can collect logs from every application container that uses the json-file log driver. Amazon ECS keeps each container's logs in a dedicated directory named with the container ID and retains them until the container is removed, so your managed daemon can use native file-based log collection and trace every log back to the container that produced it. To get started, set the log driver to json-file in the logConfiguration of your application task definition. Next, register a daemon task definition that specifies a volume with logDriverVolumeConfiguration, and mount the volume into your daemon container using mountPoints. You can configure this using the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, API, AWS SDKs or AWS CloudFormation. This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon ECS Managed Instances and Managed Daemons are available, at no additional cost. To learn more, refer to our documentation page and visit Amazon ECS Managed Instances .

items.title: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) is now available in the Asia Pacific (Taipei) and Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Regions
items.description: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) is now available in the Asia Pacific (Taipei) and Asia Pacific (New Zealand) Regions, adding to the list of  available Regions where you can use Amazon DocumentDB. Amazon DocumentDB is a fully managed, native JSON database that makes it simple and cost-effective to operate critical document workloads at virtually any scale without managing infrastructure. Amazon DocumentDB is designed to give you the scalability and durability you need when operating mission-critical MongoDB workloads. In addition, Amazon DocumentDB natively integrates with Amazon CloudWatch, AWS CloudTrail, AWS Lambda, AWS Backup, and more. Amazon DocumentDB supports millions of requests per second and can be scaled out to 15 low-latency read replicas in minutes with no application downtime. To learn more about Amazon DocumentDB, please visit the Amazon DocumentDB  product page and pricing page . You can create an Amazon DocumentDB cluster from the AWS Management Console , AWS Command Line Interface (CLI) , or AWS SDKs.

items.title: AWS Sign-In now supports OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange
items.description: AWS Sign-In now supports OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), enabling applications to exchange third-party OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens for short-lived, AWS service-scoped OAuth access tokens. This allows customers to securely integrate third-party applications with supported AWS services without sharing AWS credentials, while maintaining access controls through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). This capability is available for supported AWS services that use AWS Sign-In OAuth , enabling customers to use existing identity providers to securely access AWS services without managing additional credentials. To learn more , see the AWS Sign-In User Guide , AWS MCP Server User Guide and the AWS Glue launch announcement .

items.title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports copying option groups during cross-Region snapshot copy
items.description: Amazon RDS for Oracle now lets you copy the option group associated with a DB snapshot when you copy that snapshot to another AWS Region. Amazon RDS for Oracle uses option groups to enable and configure features that make it simple to manage your databases. Option groups are specific to the AWS Region where you create them. Previously, customers wanting to replicate RDS backups that had option groups to a different AWS Region had to copy the snapshot without the option group and then recreate the option group in the target Region before restoring the snapshot. Now, you no longer need to separate the steps and can instead initiate the snapshot copy and specify the option group copy in the same request as the snapshot copy. The existing boolean parameter CopyOptionGroup on the CopyDBSnapshot API and CLI commands now also support cross-Region copy, along with cross-account copy. You can now copy options groups to the destination snapshot in the target AWS Region from the source snapshot by setting this parameter to true . This capability is available on Amazon RDS for Oracle in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, review the Amazon RDS API Documentation .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer now shows associated cases in contact records
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer now includes case IDs and reference numbers in contact records, helping supervisors and analysts understand which customer issues drive contact volume. Cases track issues, such as refund requests or billing disputes, across interactions and teams. Supervisors can now identify the cases associated with an interaction directly on the Contact Details page without searching individual cases. Analysts can access the same information through the DescribeContact API and contact event streams to measure the number of interactions per case. Cases is available in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, visit the Cases webpage and documentation .

items.title: AWS announces AWS Interconnect - last mile preview with Equinix
items.description: AWS Interconnect - last mile is now available in preview with Equinix. You can connect your infrastructure across Equinix's global network of 282 data centers worldwide to AWS in a few clicks. Interconnect - last mile gives you managed, private, and resilient connections to AWS, so you don't have to order cross-connects or configure routers. To set up in the AWS Management Console, choose an AWS Region, a bandwidth speed, a Direct Connect gateway, and your Equinix Fabric One project ID. AWS generates an activation key, which you enter in the Equinix Fabric One portal to complete the setup. You can also initiate the connection from the Equinix Fabric One portal. AWS and Equinix set up quad-redundant capacity in advance, across two locations and four separate links, with BGP peering, VLANs and ASNs configured for you. Every connection is built for maximum resilience and comes with a 99.99% availability SLA. Traffic between AWS and Equinix edge devices is encrypted with MACsec by default. During the preview, you can order 1 Gbps Interconnect - last mile connections at no charge to the US West (N. California) Region through the San Jose metro and to the US East (N. Virginia) Region through the Northern Virginia metro. When Interconnect - last mile with Equinix becomes generally available, you'll be able to scale bandwidth from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps in the console. You can create connections using the console, the AWS CLI, or the API. Partners can integrate using the open API package on GitHub . To learn more, see the AWS Interconnect - last mile documentation .

items.title: Amazon EC2 and VPC now display related resources for all resource types
items.description: Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), and AWS Global View now display related resources for all resource types in their consoles. Previously, only security groups had an option to view related resources. Now you can see relationships for all EC2 and VPC resource types, including EC2 instances, Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes, Launch Templates, Auto Scaling groups, subnets, route tables, and more. The Related Resources tab has also been moved to the console toolbar for easier access. This capability helps you better understand your infrastructure dependencies and troubleshoot issues more efficiently. For example, when investigating an EC2 instance issue, you can quickly view its associated EBS volumes, security groups, subnets, and route tables without navigating between multiple console pages. Network administrators can now trace connections from a subnet to its associated route tables, network ACLs, and instances, streamlining network configuration reviews and security audits. This feature is now available in all commercial AWS Regions. To learn more, visit Amazon EC2 and Amazon VPC in the AWS Management Console .

items.title: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode supports OpenID Connect (OIDC) for Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure
items.description: AWS DataSync Enhanced mode now supports OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication for Google Cloud Storage and Microsoft Azure Blob Storage locations. DataSync uses an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to get short-lived credentials from Google Cloud or Microsoft Entra ID and refreshes them automatically so your transfers run without interruption. You can now use DataSync to access your Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage without long-term credentials such as hash-based message authentication code (HMAC) keys or shared access signature (SAS) tokens. This lets you move data across clouds while complying with security policies that might prohibit long-term credentials. You can get started by adding an IAM role to your DataSync location with the AWS CLI, API, or AWS CloudFormation. This capability is available in all AWS Regions where DataSync Enhanced mode is supported. To learn more, visit the AWS DataSync User Guide .

items.title: Amazon S3 Tables now provide a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization
items.description: Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Iceberg adds ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel to your data lake, but moving off Hive usually means building a migration pipeline for each table, which can take weeks. You can now let S3 Tables manage your migration, resulting in query-ready Iceberg tables that stay optimized as data grows. S3 Tables validate, convert, and copy your data while production workloads keep running. To lower migration risk, you can review each step, sync destination tables with source changes as often as you need, or roll back to your source data. You pay only for the data that the job copies, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier. If your tables use Snappy compression, S3 Tables recompress them to Zstandard (ZSTD) and compact them, which reduces storage and object count and improves query performance. To get started, visit the AWS Management Console or use the Amazon S3 Tables migration APIs. A migration skill is also available in the Agent Toolkit for AWS to help AI agents orchestrate the workflow autonomously. At launch, S3 Tables managed migration supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. It is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm). For pricing information visit Amazon S3 pricing . To learn more, see the Amazon S3 Tables overview page , documentation , and AWS News Blog .

items.title: RHEL 10, Rocky 10 and Ubuntu 26.04 Bundles for WorkSpaces
items.description: AWS announces new Linux bundles for Amazon WorkSpaces Personal, including Rocky Linux 10, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. With these bundles, you can launch WorkSpaces on the latest enterprise Linux operating systems and use newer software packages that are only available in these releases. These new bundles feature modern Wayland display technology, giving you access to the latest Linux desktop capabilities. The new OS options also bring stronger security and longer support lifecycles from each distribution. While Rocky Linux 8 and 9, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and 9, and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and 24.04 LTS powered WorkSpaces bundles remain available, the new bundles let you adopt the latest releases on your own timeline. Your existing WorkSpaces keep running with no changes. You can move users to the new operating systems once your applications and workflows are ready. To get started, select a managed Rocky Linux 10, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, or Ubuntu 26.04 LTS bundle when you create a new Linux WorkSpace. These bundles are available in Standard, Performance, Power, and PowerPro sizes in all AWS Regions where Amazon WorkSpaces is available. For a full list of supported operating systems, see Bundles and images for WorkSpaces Personal . For pricing information, visit the Amazon WorkSpaces pricing page .

items.title: New features for Amazon EC2 Capacity Manager
items.description: Amazon EC2 Capacity Manager now offers real-time supportability checks and capacity fulfillment metrics. Real-time supportability checks help customers find capacity by scoring how well each instance type and Availability Zone can support a request, without launching or reserving instances. Capacity fulfillment metrics show how much capacity was delivered against the amount requested. Global enterprises that run thousands of workloads across hundreds of accounts often spread each one across multiple instance types and Availability Zones, giving Amazon EC2 more options to fulfill each request. Starting today, customers can use the supportability checks in Capacity Manager to understand which Availability Zones and instance types give them the best chance of getting the capacity they need. The check returns a High, Medium, or Low score for each option, plus an overall score. Additionally, with fulfillment metrics, customers can measure fulfillment rates across their AWS organization, accounts, Regions, and tagged workloads, with a breakdown by instance type and Availability Zone, to show how well those choices are working. Both capabilities are included with AWS Unified Operations , the AWS Support plan for global enterprises running mission-critical workloads, and are available in all commercial AWS Regions. To learn more, read Plan and measure EC2 flexibility with Amazon EC2 Capacity Manager  on the AWS Compute Blog and see the Amazon EC2 Capacity Manager user guide . To get started, visit the Capacity Manager console .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause and resume emails
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer lets agents pause emails while waiting for information or approvals, freeing them to handle higher-priority contacts and resume their work later. For example, an agent waiting for a supervisor to approve a refund can pause the email and take an incoming call. Paused time is tracked separately from active handling time, giving supervisors a more accurate view of the time agents spend working on emails. Agents can pause and resume emails directly from the Agent Workspace or Contact Control Panel (CCP) and see how long each email has been paused. Supervisors can monitor paused emails and pause duration in real time, and use flows to automatically resume or transfer emails that remain paused beyond a configured threshold. Amazon Connect Customer email pause and resume is available in the US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Africa (Cape Town), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), and Europe (London) regions . To learn more and get started, please refer to the help documentation or visit the Amazon Connect Customer website.

items.title: Amazon WorkSpaces for AI agents now supports Linux and Windows 11 cloud desktops
items.description: WorkSpaces for AI agents now supports Linux and Windows 11 cloud desktops, in addition to Windows Server. You can run each AI agent on the operating system that its workflows and applications require. Your agents can then work in the same environments that your workforce already uses, without re-platforming.  Linux desktops give agents full root access to the operating system where many developers already build, test, and automate agentic workflows. Agents can take on developer tasks, such as running builds, tests, and scripts, within the enterprise-grade security and governance controls you already rely on. Windows 11 desktops let agents work in the enterprise applications your teams depend on every day. Linux and Windows 11 desktops have the same security and governance controls as Windows Server desktops. These include network isolation, IAM-based access, and the compliance boundaries your organization already has in place. To get started operating AI agents on WorkSpaces, visit: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/appstream2/latest/developerguide/agent-access.html .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer prefills the email address for new threads started from cases
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer automatically fills in the customer’s email address from the linked customer profile when agents start a new email thread from a case. This saves agents time and reduces manual entry errors by eliminating the need to look up or type the address. Cases is available in the following AWS regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, visit the Cases webpage and documentation .

items.title: AWS Config now supports 10 new resource types
items.description: AWS Config now supports 10 additional AWS resource types across key services including Amazon ElastiCache and Amazon QuickSight. This expansion provides greater coverage over your AWS environment, enabling you to more effectively discover, assess, audit, and remediate an even broader range of resources. With this launch, if you have enabled recording for all resource types, then AWS Config will automatically track these new additions. The newly supported resource types are also available in Config rules and Config aggregators. You can now use AWS Config to monitor the following newly supported resource types in all AWS Regions where the resources are available: Resource Types: AWS::Billing::BillingView AWS::MPA::IdentitySource AWS::Connect::HoursOfOperation AWS::Notifications::OrganizationalUnitAssociation AWS::ElastiCache::CacheCluster AWS::NotificationsContacts::EmailContact AWS::ElastiCache::ReplicationGroup AWS::Oam::Link AWS::MediaLive::SignalMap AWS::QuickSight::Agent

items.title: Amazon RDS now supports the latest Cumulative Update and GDR updates for Microsoft SQL Server
items.description: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for SQL Server now supports the latest Cumulative Updates (CU) and General Distribution Release (GDR) updates for Microsoft SQL Server. This release includes support for Microsoft SQL Server 2017 CU31+GDR KB5128496 (RDS version 14.00.3560.2.v1), SQL Server 2019 CU32+GDR KB5128494 (RDS version 15.00.4500.2.v1), SQL Server 2022 CU27+GDR KB5126934 (RDS version 16.00.4305.5.v1) and SQL Server 2025 CU10 KB5125471 (RDS version 17.00.5035.5.v1). For additional information on the improvements and fixes included in these updates, see Microsoft documentation for KB5128496, KB5128494, KB5126934 and KB5125471. We recommend that you upgrade your Amazon RDS for SQL Server instances to apply these updates using Amazon RDS Management Console, or by using the AWS SDK or CLI. You can learn more about upgrading your database instance in the Amazon RDS SQL Server User Guide for upgrading your RDS Microsoft SQL Server DB engine .

items.title: Amazon CloudWatch now supports API keys for OpenTelemetry traces
items.description: Amazon CloudWatch now supports bearer token authentication, using API keys (bearer tokens), as an additional option for sending OpenTelemetry traces to the AWS X-Ray OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) traces endpoint. Any OTLP/HTTP client that can set an Authorization header, including the OpenTelemetry Collector and OpenTelemetry SDK exporters, can now authenticate with a bearer token instead of signing requests with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4). This helps teams send traces from workloads that can't use the AWS SDK or short-term credentials, such as applications running on premises or in other clouds, CI/CD pipelines, and third-party tools that support only a static Authorization header. SigV4 remains the recommended authentication method for sending traces to CloudWatch, and the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDKs continue to use SigV4 by default with no changes required. Traces sent with either method get the same CloudWatch capabilities, including Transaction Search, Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals, and Amazon CloudWatch Omni. Bearer token authentication for traces is available in all commercial AWS Regions where the AWS X-Ray OTLP traces endpoint is available. To learn more, see Setting up bearer token authentication for traces in the AWS X-Ray Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS Transform for mainframe improves the reimagine modernization workflow
items.description: AWS Transform for mainframe now discovers business functions with field-level precision and generates a new requirements coverage report in the assess and reimagine workflow. Previously, business functions that used the same table or file were grouped together, and you had to build your own traceability reporting from AWS Transform artifacts. With this launch, you can start modernizing z/OS COBOL and PL/I workloads from a more accurate catalog of business functions and verify requirements coverage before you build. Business functions are now grouped only when they affect the same data fields. They also include screens and queues and carry clearer names and descriptions. The new requirements coverage report shows how every part of your application is accounted for in the generated requirements. Every line of source code is classified by how it was handled, every business rule links to the exact lines it came from, and every requirement is backed by the business rules that support it. You can review coverage from the full portfolio down to a single line before moving into forward engineering in Kiro and other IDEs. These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform for mainframe is available. For more information, see the AWS Region table . To learn more, visit AWS Transform for mainframe or see the AWS Transform for mainframe documentation .

items.title: Amazon EKS Capabilities now supports Argo CD Notifications
items.description: The Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Capability for Argo CD now supports Argo CD Notifications, providing notifications when your applications sync, fail, or change health. You define triggers and message templates in your cluster and subscribe individual Applications with an annotation, the same way you do in upstream Argo CD. With this launch, you can deliver notifications to 16 notification services, including Slack, PagerDuty, Opsgenie, Amazon SQS, and Amazon EventBridge. The Amazon SQS and Amazon EventBridge services authenticate with your IAM Capability Role, so you can route deployment events into your own event-driven workflows without storing credentials in your cluster. For a service that requires third-party credentials such as a Slack token, you can specify an AWS Secrets Manager ARN in place of the secret and EKS will automatically use it on your behalf. Notifications are available in all AWS Regions where the EKS Capability for Argo CD is available, at no additional charge. Standard charges apply for resources related to the services your notifications use, for example Amazon SQS or Amazon EventBridge. To learn more, visit Amazon EKS  and refer to the Amazon EKS User Guide .

items.title: Amazon RDS for Oracle now supports M8i and R8i instances in additional AWS Regions
items.description: Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle  now supports M8i and R8i instances in additional AWS Regions. Both M8i and R8i instances are now available in Asia Pacific (New Zealand) and Canada West (Calgary), and R8i instances are now available in Europe (Milan, Stockholm, and Zurich) and Israel (Tel Aviv). These instances are powered by custom Intel Xeon 6 processors, available only on AWS, delivering the highest performance and fastest memory bandwidth among comparable Intel processors in the cloud. The M8i and R8i instances offer up to 15% better price-performance, and 2.5x more memory bandwidth compared to previous generation Intel-based instances. M8i and R8i instances are available for Amazon RDS for Oracle in Bring Your Own License model for Oracle Database Enterprise Edition (EE) and Oracle Database Standard Edition 2 (SE2). For EE, instances are available in sizes from large to 48xlarge, as well as bare metal sizes metal-48xl and metal-96xl. For SE2, instances are available in sizes from large to 4xlarge and bare metal sizes metal-48xl and metal-96xl. Refer to Amazon RDS for Oracle Pricing for available instance configurations, pricing, and region availability.

items.title: Haiku 5.5 now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
items.description: A new Anthropic model is now available in the Kiro IDE and CLI for the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. With Haiku 5.5, all three Claude 5.5 models are now available in Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US). Claude Haiku 5.5 is the fastest model in the Claude 5.5 family. It's a clear step up from Claude Haiku 4.5, built for work that runs in large volumes and needs quick responses. Developers can use it to summarize and compact long context, classify and route requests, process text in bulk, and make small, targeted edits across many files. It also works well as a review subagent that runs in parallel, while Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 take on harder planning and coding work. Haiku 5.5 uses adaptive thinking across five effort levels from low to max, with medium as the default. It's available with a 1M context window and a 0.06x credit multiplier. Requests over 100K tokens are billed at a 0.3x multiplier. Ensure your IDE or CLI is updated to the latest version, then restart it to access the new model from the model selector. For more details, visit the GovCloud documentation , the monitoring and tracking guide , or contact your AWS account team. To learn more about Kiro, visit the Kiro product page .

items.title: Amazon RDS now supports per snapshot billing
items.description: Starting today, Amazon RDS supports per snapshot billing for Amazon RDS snapshots. Per snapshot billing allows you to get the cost of each individual snapshot. Previously, RDS snapshot charges were aggregated at the database instance level on the Cost and Usage report as well as the Cost Explorer. This meant that while understanding the snapshot charges, you could only see the aggregate view at the database instance instead of drilling down to each individual snapshot. Now, you can use cost allocation tags on your snapshots to see exactly how much each snapshot costs, giving you a better understanding of your backups spend and budgets. Per snapshot billing is enabled by default on all RDS snapshots for no additional charge. Per snapshot billing is available for all Amazon RDS engines in all commercial AWS Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. To learn more, please visit our documentation .

items.title: Amazon Quick on desktop now uses your organization's existing Amazon Quick sign-in
items.description: For organizations that use Amazon Quick, the desktop application now signs users in with the same sign-in method the organization already uses for Quick on the web. Administrators no longer need to register an OIDC application in their identity provider or set up separate desktop sign-in before users can get started. If a user can sign in to Quick on the web, that user can sign in to the desktop application. To turn on desktop access, an administrator adds the desktop connector once in the Amazon Quick console. Users then enter their Quick account name, choose Sign In, and finish signing in through their browser. This works for accounts that use IAM Identity Center, IAM federation, or native Amazon Quick users. If your organization wants to manage desktop sign-in separately, you can still set up a dedicated identity provider configuration with providers such as Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace, Okta, or Ping Identity. Amazon Quick on desktop is available in AWS Regions that support the full Amazon Quick feature set . To get started, see Amazon Quick on desktop in the Amazon Quick User Guide.

items.title: Amazon Aurora MySQL 8.4.10 is now generally available
items.description: Starting today, Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition 8.4 supports MySQL 8.4.10. We recommend upgrading to the newer minor versions to accept fixes for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) in prior versions of MySQL and to benefit from bug fixes, performance improvements, and new functionality added by the MySQL community. For more details, refer to the Aurora MySQL 8.4 and MySQL 8.4.10 release notes. Aurora MySQL 8.4.10 adds support for global transaction identifiers (GTID) tags, which lets you assign a user-defined tag to GTIDs to help you identify and group related transactions in binary log replication. This release also adds support for a maximum of 50,000 simultaneous connections per DB instance, which allows connection-intensive applications to scale without adding a connection pooling layer. Learn more about maximum connections best practices in the Amazon Aurora MySQL User Guide .   You can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable automatic minor version upgrades and use the AWS Organizations Upgrade Rollout Policy to orchestrate upgrades across your clusters in phases, validating on lower-priority environments before upgrading your most critical ones. You can perform minor version upgrades in-place or via snapshot restore. Learn more about performing version upgrades in the Amazon Aurora User Guide . This release is supported in all AWS Regions where Aurora MySQL is available. Amazon Aurora is designed for high performance and availability at global scale with full MySQL compatibility. It provides scale-to-zero serverless compute, Aurora Global Database for multi-Region resilience, Aurora I/O-Optimized for improved price performance on I/O-intensive workloads, and built-in security and continuous backups. To get started, take a look at Aurora's getting started page .

items.title: AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources
items.description: AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event source mappings (ESM), for Kafka clusters that customers run themselves and for managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. Customers can now scale processing for Kafka workloads beyond the partition count of a topic, increasing throughput during traffic spikes and improving processing resilience. Customers building event-driven Kafka workloads for use cases such as image and video encoding, fraud detection, notification delivery, and telemetry ingestion treat each event as an independent unit of work, where processing speed matters more than strict ordering. Previously, Kafka ESMs used the Kafka consumer group protocol, which assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a consumer group. Customers needing higher parallelism had to over-partition topics or move traffic to a separate queuing system, adding infrastructure to operate and producer code to maintain. Queue support for self-managed Kafka ESMs is built on Kafka share groups, which are generally available in Apache Kafka 4.2. This launch enables multiple event pollers to consume concurrently from the same partition, with each event poller supporting up to 10 concurrent invocations. This decouples parallelism from partition count with no changes to producers, topic configuration, or function code. As a result, customers get higher throughput during traffic spikes and more resilient processing, because a slow or failed event no longer holds up other events in the same partition. Queue mode does not preserve partition ordering and is intended for workloads that do not require it. This capability requires a Kafka cluster with share groups enabled, such as Apache Kafka 4.2 or later, and is available in all AWS commercial Regions where self-managed Kafka ESM is available. To get started, create a self-managed Kafka ESM with ConsumptionMode set to Queue through the AWS Management Console, Lambda API, AWS CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS SAM, or AWS CDK. Standard Lambda pricing applies. Customers who configure provisioned mode for their self-managed Kafka ESM also pay for Event Poller Unit (EPU) usage. To learn more, see the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and AWS Lambda pricing .

items.title: Amazon Aurora MySQL 3.14 (compatible with MySQL 8.0.46) is generally available
items.description: Starting today, Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition 3 (compatible with MySQL 8.0) supports MySQL 8.0.46, which includes community MySQL fixes and Aurora-specific improvements. In addition to operational improvements, Aurora MySQL 3.14 introduces support for post-quantum TLS (PQ-TLS) key exchange, providing you with post-quantum cryptography options for encrypting your data in-transit. For detailed information on this release, refer to Aurora MySQL 3 and MySQL 8.0.46 release notes. You can upgrade your databases during scheduled maintenance windows using automatic minor version upgrades. To simplify operations at scale, enable automatic minor version upgrades and use the AWS Organizations Upgrade Rollout Policy to orchestrate upgrades across your clusters in phases. You can perform minor version upgrades in-place or via snapshot restore. This release is supported in all AWS Regions where Aurora MySQL is available. Amazon Aurora is designed for high performance and availability at global scale with full MySQL compatibility. It provides scale-to-zero serverless compute, Aurora Global Database for multi-Region resilience, Aurora I/O-Optimized for improved price performance on I/O-intensive workloads, and built-in security and continuous backups. To get started, take a look at Aurora’s getting started page .

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools in flows
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer now enables you to invoke Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools in customer experience flows through the new 'External Tool' block. With this launch, you can connect flows to third-party applications through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway and reuse the same tools used by your agentic experiences to retrieve data or trigger actions, without writing custom Lambda functions. For example, when a customer contacts a financial institution about a recent transaction, a flow can use the External Tool block to retrieve relevant context from a third-party application, such as case history from their CRM system, or transaction details from a banking platform. This feature is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo). To learn more about this feature, refer to the administrator guide . To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the Amazon Connect Customer website.

items.title: Amazon Connect Customer now supports Cases and External Tool events in the Wait block
items.description: Amazon Connect Customer now supports Cases and External Tool events in the Wait block, giving you more control over how your customer experience flows react to real-time data changes. In addition to waiting for a Lambda function to complete, you can now wait until a Connect Case field meets a specified condition or an External Tool invocation completes. This enables you to wait for critical information before advancing an interaction, reducing unnecessary transfers and saving time for both your end-customers and agents. For example, you can hold a flow until a refund status field is updated on a case, then automatically resume and route the interaction based on the outcome.  To learn more about this feature, refer to the administrator guide and availability of Connect Customer features by Region . To learn more about Amazon Connect Customer, an agentic AI solution that helps enterprises deliver exceptional customer experiences, visit the Amazon Connect Customer website.

items.title: EC2 Amazon Machine Images can now be scanned for vulnerabilities through Amazon Inspector
items.description: Amazon Inspector now extends its vulnerability scanning to EC2 Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), enabling you to identify software vulnerabilities in your AMIs without launching instances or installing additional software. This helps you fix issues at the source before AMIs are used to launch instances across your fleet. With this capability, you can run continuous evaluations to monitor your AMI catalog for newly discovered vulnerabilities, or perform targeted one-time scans for specific AMIs directly from the EC2 Console. You can enable AMI scanning for an account or across your entire organization in Amazon Inspector. For AWS Security Hub customers, you can enable AMI scanning as an add-on across your organization, and findings are also delivered to Security Hub. Based on the scan results, you can enable the Allowed AMIs setting and specify security criteria that AMIs must meet to be available within your account and enforce this setting across the entire organization using Declarative Policies. Customers building AMIs with EC2 Image Builder can integrate scanning directly into their pipelines and restrict distribution of AMIs that do not meet their security standards. AMI Scanning helps you detect and remediate vulnerabilities earlier in your deployment pipeline, reducing the risk of deploying compromised compute resources. Security teams can now establish a consistent vulnerability scanning process across all AMIs improving their security posture before instances are launched. This capability is available in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon Inspector is available. To learn more, see the EC2 User Guide ,  Amazon Inspector User Guide , the Amazon Inspector pricing page , and the Amazon Inspector product page .

items.title: Amazon Textract now available in Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich)
items.description: Amazon Textract is now available in the Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich) Regions. Amazon Textract is a machine learning service that automatically extracts text, handwriting, and data from scanned documents, going beyond simple optical character recognition (OCR) to identify and extract text and structured data. At launch in these Regions, Amazon Textract supports text detection and document analysis. This includes the DetectDocumentText, AnalyzeDocument, StartDocumentTextDetection, GetDocumentTextDetection, StartDocumentAnalysis, and GetDocumentAnalysis operations. The AnalyzeExpense, AnalyzeID, and AnalyzeLending operations, and Custom Queries (adapters), are not available in these Regions at this time. With this launch, Amazon Textract is available in a total of 18 AWS Regions: US East (Ohio), US East (N. Virginia), US West (N. California), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Europe (Paris), Europe (Spain), the AWS GovCloud (US-East) and AWS GovCloud (US-West) Regions, and the newly added Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich) Regions. To learn more, see the Amazon Textract product page and the Amazon Textract Developer Guide . For pricing and Region availability, see the Amazon Textract pricing page and Amazon Textract endpoints and quotas .

items.title: Announcing AWS for Fluent Bit 3.0.0 based on Fluent Bit 4.1.1
items.description: AWS for Fluent Bit announces version 3.0.0 , based on Fluent Bit version 4.1.1 and Amazon Linux 2023. Container logging using AWS for Fluent Bit is now more performant and more feature-rich for AWS customers, including those using Amazon Elastic Container Services (Amazon ECS) and Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). AWS for Fluent Bit enables Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS customers to collect, process, and route container logs to destinations including Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, and Amazon S3 without changing application code. AWS for Fluent Bit 3.0.0 upgrades the Fluent Bit version to 4.1.1, and upgrades the base image to Amazon Linux 2023. These updates deliver access to the latest Fluent Bit features, significant performance improvements, and enhanced security. New features include native OpenTelemetry (OTel) support for ingesting and forwarding OTLP logs, metrics, and traces with AWS SigV4 authentication. Performance improvements include faster JSON parsing, processing more logs per vCPU with lower latency. Security enhancements include TLS min version and cipher controls, which enforce your TLS policy on outputs from AWS for Fluent Bit for stronger protocol posture. You can use AWS for Fluent Bit 3.0.0 on both ECS and EKS. On ECS, update the FireLens log-router container image in your task definition to the 3.0.0 tag from the Amazon ECR Public Gallery. On EKS, upgrade by either updating the Helm release or setting the DaemonSet image to the 3.0.0 version. The AWS for Fluent Bit image is available in the Amazon ECR Public Gallery and in the Amazon ECR repository. You can also find it on GitHub for source code and additional guidance.   10/29/2025 - This post has been updated to accurately reflect the Fluent Bit version at launch. 11/02/2026 - This post has been updated to clarify the scope of OpenTelemetry support.

items.title: Announcing an updated text detection model for Amazon Textract
items.description: Amazon Textract now provides an updated text detection model that improves accuracy, expands language support, and enhances multilingual table extraction. The updated model applies to the DetectDocumentText and AnalyzeDocument APIs and requires no changes to your Amazon Textract API requests or response schema. Your applications are served by the updated model automatically, so you can continue calling Amazon Textract exactly as before. The updated model expands language coverage to more than 40 languages, including Albanian, Arabic, Basque, Belarusian, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Finnish, French, German, Hebrew, Hindi, Hungarian, Icelandic, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Latvian, Lithuanian, Luxembourgish, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Serbian Cyrillic, Serbian Latin, Slovak, Slovenian, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish, Turkmen, and Ukrainian, enabling reliable processing of previously unsupported scripts. Accuracy improvements include enhanced long-word recognition and handwriting detection. Additionally, multilingual table extraction is more robust on merged cells, skewed or rotated tables, and partial or corrupted tables. These improvements help you accurately process invoices, forms, identity documents, and other multilingual or complex documents, including those with tables, at scale. The updated Amazon Textract model is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon Textract is available. To learn more, see the Amazon Textract product page and the Amazon Textract Developer Guide .

items.title: Amazon CloudFront now supports self-service increases in AWS Service Quotas
items.description: Amazon CloudFront now supports AWS Service Quotas, so you can view, monitor, and request increases for 28 CloudFront quotas from the Service Quotas console or API. Until now, increasing a quota on resources such as distributions, cache policies, origins, or alternate domain names meant opening a support case and waiting for manual review. If you have AWS Business Support or higher, requests for limit increases within published thresholds are now approved automatically. For example, you can raise your distribution quota from 500 to 1,000, or the number of alternate domain names per distribution from 100 to 500, without opening a support case. Some quotas also publish usage metrics to Amazon CloudWatch every 5 minutes, so you can set alarms and request an increase before you reach a limit.. This feature is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudFront is supported. To get started, visit the Service Quotas console to view and request increases for your CloudFront quotas. To learn more, see Amazon CloudFront quotas in the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide.

items.title: AWS Compute Optimizer now supports additional Amazon EC2 instance types in the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions
items.description: AWS Compute Optimizer now provides rightsizing recommendations for 389 additional Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance types in AWS GovCloud (US-West) and 276 in AWS GovCloud (US-East) Regions. Customers running regulated and government workloads can find the same cost and performance opportunities on current-generation instance types without manual analysis. Compute Optimizer has expanded support to include the latest generation families in every workload category. The additions include Compute Optimized (C7i, C7i-flex, C8g, C8gn), General Purpose (M7i, M7i-flex, M8g, M8gd, M8i, M8i-flex), Memory Optimized (R7i, R8g, R8gd, R8i, R8i-flex), Memory Intensive (X2iedn, X8i), and Storage Optimized (I7i, I7ie, I8g, I8ge) instance types. With this expansion, Compute Optimizer supports 724 instance types across 102 families in AWS GovCloud (US-West) and 542 instance types across 69 families in AWS GovCloud (US-East), in both EC2 instance and EC2 Auto Scaling group recommendations. This expanded coverage is available today at no additional cost in the AWS GovCloud (US-West) and AWS GovCloud (US-East) Regions. You can start using Compute Optimizer through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDK. To learn more, see the AWS Compute Optimizer product page and AWS Compute Optimizer in the AWS GovCloud (US) User Guide .

items.title: Amazon Bedrock expands API support and introduces Cross-Region Inferencing for OpenAI models in AWS GovCloud (US)
items.description: Amazon Bedrock now supports the OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Terra and Luna) on the bedrock-runtime endpoint, with support for the Responses, Converse, and Chat Completions APIs in AWS GovCloud (US). It also adds support for Cross-Region Inference, allowing customers to use Cross-Region Inference within AWS GovCloud (US) regions to access higher throughput and increased redundancy.   Cross-Region Inference automatically routes inference requests across both AWS GovCloud (US) Regions to give you higher throughput, without you needing to manage capacity across multiple Regions. Cross-Region Inference within AWS GovCloud (US) routes requests across both regions so you can scale while maintaining US data sovereignty, giving you the broadest access to Bedrock capacity and the highest throughput during demand spikes. This launch also expands API support; you can use OpenAI GPT models with the Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Converse API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint. Because these native OpenAI APIs now run on bedrock-runtime, the models work with the same account-level controls you already use for other models on Bedrock: usage appears in Bedrock model invocation logging (deliverable to Amazon S3 or Amazon CloudWatch Logs) and in Amazon CloudWatch metrics covering invocation counts, token counts, latency, throttles, and errors, and it is itemized in AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report so you can attribute spend by model. Cross-Region Inference for OpenAI models is available in all AWS Regions where OpenAI models on Amazon Bedrock are offered. To get started, review the model cards for GPT-5.6 (Terra and Luna) in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

items.title: Web Search now available on Kiro in AWS GovCloud (US)
items.description: Kiro web search gives the agent real-time access to current information on the internet, so its answers draw on up-to-date search results and page content. The agent uses web search automatically when a question involves recent changes or topics beyond the model's training data. Answers that use web results include citations. Kiro enterprise administrators can turn off web search and web fetch for their organization from the Kiro console under Settings. Teams can also remove web tools from individual custom agents, or block them with capability-based permission rules. For more details, visit the  AWS GovCloud (US) documentation , the monitoring and tracking guide , or contact your AWS account team. To learn more about Kiro, visit the Kiro product page .
